title: Finding Patterns in Lived Experience
answer: Finding patterns in lived experience is the work of turning interviews, diaries, focus groups, open-ended survey answers, and observation notes into themes, categories, or narratives that describe how people understand their world. It sits inside qualitative analysis and mixed methods, where the aim is depth and context rather than statistical generalization. A single case can matter, and a pattern is often a recurring meaning rather than a frequency count. Researchers may combine these accounts with numbers later, but the starting point is the person's own words and the sense they make of events.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Finding patterns in lived experience is the work of turning interviews, diaries, focus groups, open-ended survey answers, and observation notes into themes, categories, or narratives that describe how people understand their world. It sits inside qualitative analysis and mixed methods, where the aim is depth and context rather than statistical generalization. A single case can matter, and a pattern is often a recurring meaning rather than a frequency count. Researchers may combine these accounts with numbers later, but the starting point is the person's own words and the sense they make of events.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of transcription software, qualitative data analysis packages such as NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA, or Dedoose, and plain tools like spreadsheets and word processors. Audio and video recordings are turned into text, then coded and annotated, often with memos attached to each passage. The site's catalogue lists 732 AI tools, and some of these can suggest codes, cluster similar passages, or detect topics, but they do not replace close reading. Secure storage and clear file naming are part of the infrastructure because the material is often sensitive.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually begins with a research question, then data collection through interviews, focus groups, or written accounts, followed by close reading and coding. Researchers may use inductive coding, where themes emerge from the material, or deductive coding, where a framework guides the analysis, and often they combine both. Memos, reflexive journals, and team discussions help test whether a pattern is real or an artifact of the analyst's assumptions. In mixed methods designs, these themes are later linked to survey results, outcomes, or other numbers through joint displays or triangulation. The site's library of 135 research papers and 12,233 claims extracted from research works can provide examples of how others have handled coding and theme development.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this work centre on consent, privacy, and the potential for harm when personal accounts are analysed. Transcripts and recordings are sensitive, so anonymisation, secure storage, and clear data retention rules are essential, and participants should know how their words will be used. Provenance matters because a theme must be traceable back to the original passage, and the site's policy of linking to the original paper rather than a search tool reflects that principle. AI tools add risk if they send data to external servers or if their suggestions are treated as findings without human review. Researchers also need to document their coding decisions and any software used so that others can follow the chain of evidence.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more transparent use of AI for transcription, initial coding, and pattern detection, while keeping interpretation in human hands. Larger language models can summarise long transcripts or suggest themes, but they also risk flattening nuance and importing bias from their training data. Mixed methods designs are likely to integrate computational text analysis with traditional close reading, and reporting standards will need to say exactly where a machine helped and where a person decided. The site's catalogue of 797 scientific models and 732 AI tools shows how many options are emerging, and its 686 glossary terms reflect a growing shared vocabulary. The next few years will probably bring better audit trails for AI-assisted coding and more debate about what counts as evidence in lived experience research.
